name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,890

clue.text: Critical about weak golf on the back of lessons

indicators.note: Riding on the back of something puts you behind it, and the back of a word is the letter it closes with.

blocks.note: the closing letter of the word, the one thing everything else rides behind
CA is circa, the Latin short form a crossword uses for approximately
a thin excuse is a weak one, the adjectives swapping straight over
golf is G in the NATO spelling alphabet, nothing to do with the sport

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a school report and the clue is four unrelated pieces. 'Golf' is the radio-alphabet letter, and 'about' is circa rather than an instruction to wrap anything round anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Critical → SCATHING: a scathing review is criticism at its most withering, so the plain adjective covers it with room to spare.

clue.text: Easy to reach sister's house where pigeon regularly nests

indicators.note: Letters picked regularly come at a steady interval — here every second one of the bird's name, counting from the second.
A bird that nests settles down inside something, so what it brings goes in the middle rather than on either end.

blocks.note: the sister is a nun, and the house she lives in with the others is a convent
every second letter of the bird, taken from the second one onwards

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sister' is the religious sense rather than a sibling, and the bird does not hand over all of itself — only the letters standing in the even places.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy to reach → CONVENIENT: a convenient shop is close at hand and no trouble to get to, which is the handy sense rather than the merely suitable one.

clue.text: Cub leader's ramble starting late with tons to carry

indicators.note: A word starting late does not begin where it should: its first letter never arrives and the rest moves up to the front.
In a down entry the load rides above whatever bears it, so the thing carried is written on top.

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for tons on any weight or cargo label
to ramble in speech is to DIGRESS, and that word here starts one letter late

explanation.walkthrough: The Scout hut is the trap. A Cub leader in Britain is the adult running a pack of Cub Scouts, but the cub here is a big cat's and its leader is its mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Cub leader → TIGRESS: a tiger cub's leader is the mother that raises and defends it, so the definition names her by the young she heads.

clue.text: Turning up halfway through test panicky is not ideal

indicators.note: In a down entry up is the direction of travel, so the run of letters is read from the bottom end back towards the top.
Halfway through the phrase is where to look: the letters sit dead centre, with three to spare on either side of them.

blocks.note: five consecutive letters straddle the space between the two words, and they run the wrong way

explanation.walkthrough: 'Panicky' reads as an anagram signal and there is nothing to shuffle: the letters are already sitting in the clue, in order, spelled from the far end.
explanation.definitionFit: not ideal → INAPT: inapt is the plain negative of apt, so something inapt is unsuited to the occasion rather than merely disappointing.

clue.text: Now newest yoga moves prevail

indicators.note: Yoga moves are changes of position, and letters that change position finish somewhere other than where the clue printed them.

blocks.note: thirteen letters of raw material — count them against the enumeration before starting

explanation.walkthrough: Thirteen letters spread over four short words are hard to see as one lump; the giveaway is that 'now newest yoga' is nonsense as English and exactly the right length.
explanation.definitionFit: prevail → GET ONE'S OWN WAY: to prevail is to have your preference win out over everyone else's, which is what the phrase describes in idiom.

clue.text: Right leaving rogue aristocrat disinherited

indicators.note: Something leaving has gone from where it stood, so the letter named just before it walks out of the word that follows.

blocks.note: R is right on a map or a dance step, and here it is the letter that goes missing
a rogue is a CUR, less the R that has just left
a toff is British slang for a posh, upper-class man

explanation.walkthrough: 'Right leaving' is an instruction rather than part of the picture — nothing here is right-wing. The rogue loses a letter and the two words are then laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: disinherited → CUT OFF: an heir cut off without a penny has been struck out of the will, which is exactly what disinheriting does.

clue.text: Staunch Titoist cleared out communist dictator's original closets

indicators.note: A room cleared out keeps only its walls, so a word cleared out keeps only the letters standing at its two ends.
To closet somebody is to shut them away in a small room, so whatever is closeted goes inside rather than alongside.

blocks.note: COMMIE is the familiar clipping of the longer word
the original letter of a word is the one it opens with
empty out the middle and the two T's at either end are all that survive

explanation.walkthrough: The politics is scenery. Tito's followers are wanted for their two outside letters only, and the dictator hands over nothing but the letter he starts with.
explanation.definitionFit: Staunch → COMMITTED: a staunch supporter is one who cannot be shifted, and that immovable loyalty is what the answer names.

clue.text: Stir cooking fat after hearing how long it lasts

indicators.note: Hearing asks for the sound of a word rather than its spelling, and after sets the next piece down behind what you have just heard.

blocks.note: how long a sentence or a school year lasts is a term, and said aloud it comes out spelled this way
the fat you fry in pours out of a bottle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stir' is prison slang as well as a commotion, which is what makes the surface hold: the sound wanted is the length of a sentence, not the cooking.
explanation.definitionFit: Stir → TURMOIL: a stir is a commotion that unsettles everyone present, and turmoil is that same confusion at full strength.

clue.text: Charge pound for love, perhaps

blocks.note: the charge a solicitor or a gallery makes is its fee
L is the pound sign £, from the Latin libra — sterling, not weight

explanation.walkthrough: Two money words build one that has nothing to do with money, and 'perhaps' is the giveaway that the definition names an example rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: love, perhaps → FEEL: loving is one instance of what a person can feel, so the general verb is defined by naming a particular emotion.

clue.text: Term for singultus? Have a go at hiccup

indicators.note: A term standing for a long word is its shorthand, and the shorthand asked for here is loose — just the single letter it opens with.

blocks.note: singultus is medical Latin for a hiccup, and only its opening letter is wanted
to have a go at somebody is to nag them, keeping on at them about something

explanation.walkthrough: The Latin is a joke on the last word — singultus is exactly what a hiccup is — but it sits in the clue for its first letter alone.
explanation.definitionFit: hiccup → SNAG: a hiccup in a plan is a small setback that interrupts it, which is the everyday figurative sense the answer carries.

clue.text: Tube connected back on Franco's heart before death

indicators.note: An across entry read back runs right to left, so the two words named before it are written from their far ends.
In an across entry a piece landing on another follows it, so the reversed pair comes after the letters it lands on.
The heart of a word is what lies at its centre, equally far from either end.

blocks.note: the two letters at the dead centre of the Spanish dictator's name
two people who connected have MET, and that word arrives the wrong way round
the Paris underground is the METRO, turned round like the piece before it

explanation.walkthrough: The Tube is a London one on the surface and a Paris one in the wordplay, and 'connected' is the past tense of meet rather than an instruction to join things up.
explanation.definitionFit: before death → ANTE MORTEM: the Latin tag means precisely that, and English keeps it for statements and injuries dated to while the patient still lived.

clue.text: Volts inside transformed the inner zoo's inescapable boundary

indicators.note: The volts go inside the material rather than parking at one end, so that letter has to be counted into what gets rearranged.
Something transformed keeps its substance and loses its shape, which is what happens to a fistful of letters.

blocks.note: V is the symbol printed on any battery for volts
eleven letters of raw material, one short of the light until the V joins them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' looks like an insertion instruction, and the V does go inside — but there is nothing to insert it into until the other eleven letters have been shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: inescapable boundary → EVENT HORIZON: it is the surface round a black hole past which nothing, not even light, can climb back out.

clue.text: See 5
Article taken from old Iranian's shelter hard to get rid of

indicators.note: What is taken from a word is subtracted out of it, so the two letters named first come out of the longer word that follows.

blocks.note: AN is one of English's three articles, and it is the one that has to go
an old Iranian is a Persian, and the possessive S counts as part of the raw material
the simplest shelter there is, canvas over a couple of poles

explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' is the grammatical kind rather than something in a newspaper, and the Persian has to be read with his apostrophe-S attached before the two letters can be lifted out.
explanation.definitionFit: hard to get rid of → PERSISTENT: a persistent cough or stain keeps coming back however often it is dealt with, which is what makes it hard to shift.

clue.text: Breakdown company tails Italian cars, ignoring Tesla

indicators.note: A car that tails another drives along behind it, so the letters named do the same and settle on the end.
What is ignored is left out altogether, so the letter named after it never joins the word at all.

blocks.note: the Italian cars are FIATS, the marque from Turin, one letter lighter
the tesla is the SI unit of magnetic flux density and its symbol is T
CO is how a company abbreviates itself on a letterhead

explanation.walkthrough: Two makes of car and both are decoys: the American one is here as a unit of measurement, and 'breakdown' is a collapse of arrangements rather than of an engine.
explanation.definitionFit: Breakdown → FIASCO: when arrangements break down completely and in public, the result is a fiasco — a total and faintly comic failure.

clue.text: Obvious method to bag runs - fielding error

indicators.note: To bag something is to put it in a bag, so the letter that follows is shut inside the word before it rather than added after it.

blocks.note: an overt act is one done in the open, which is the same as obvious
the how of a thing is the method used — the question word doing duty as a noun
R is runs on a cricket scorecard

explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'fielding error' look like an afterthought when it is the definition, and the only cricket in the wordplay is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: fielding error → OVERTHROW: in cricket an overthrow is a wild return from the field that lets the batters run again, so it names a fielder's mistake.

clue.text: Highly regarded old partner rang

blocks.note: your ex is the partner you used to have, the prefix doing duty as a noun
a bell that tolled rang slowly, one stroke at a time

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing marks the join, which is what makes a short charade hard: two everyday words end to end, with the definition in front and no link word between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Highly regarded → EXTOLLED: to extol is to praise something to the skies, and whatever gets that treatment is thereby held in high esteem.

clue.text: A certain (Liberal perhaps) North American to the west

definitions.text: A certain (Liberal perhaps) North American to the west

indicators.note: West is leftwards on the grid, so an across answer built westward is written from its last letter back towards its first.

blocks.note: NA is the standard short form of North American, and it lands back to front
perhaps is eg, for example, and that is turned round too
L is the ballot-paper abbreviation for a Liberal candidate
a certain somebody is one somebody, and it arrives the wrong way round like the rest

explanation.walkthrough: Every word does both jobs at once. Read straight the clue describes a particular westerly American; read as wordplay the same words are four abbreviations written east to west.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: this is a Los Angeles native, a North American out west, who might perfectly well be a Liberal.

clue.text: Dealing with story about case of ageism upset correspondent

indicators.note: One thing written about another goes round it, so what follows sits inside the word named before it.
A case is what encloses something, so the case of a word is the pair of letters on its outside.
Upset means overturned, and in a down entry an overturned assembly is read from the bottom of the light upwards.

blocks.note: RE heads a memo and means on the subject of, which is dealing with something
a story told to deceive is a lie, the small three-letter kind
the two letters on the outside of the word, the ones its case is made of

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dealing with' wants to be the definition, since correspondents deal with letters; it is really the two letters at the head of a memo, and the whole assembly is then read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: correspondent → EMAILER: a correspondent is simply somebody who writes to you, and these days that writing arrives electronically rather than by post.

clue.text: 15 give evidence

blocks.note: a cross-reference: the number sends you to another light in this grid for the first sense
the courtroom sense, to make a sworn statement out of court for use in one

explanation.walkthrough: A number in place of a word is a cross-reference, not an abbreviation, and the two senses share nothing but their spelling: one topples a ruler, the other swears an oath.
explanation.definitionFit: 15 → DEPOSE is to overthrow a monarch; give evidence → DEPOSE is to testify on oath, one verb doing two entirely unrelated jobs.

clue.text: Left aboard spaceship, Mike's worry reported to Houston?

indicators.note: Whatever is taken aboard is carried within the vessel, so the letter goes inside the craft's name rather than beside it.

blocks.note: an unmanned craft sent off to another planet is a probe
L is left, as on a pair of gloves or a stage direction
Mike is M in the NATO alphabet that flight crews actually speak
surface only: it nods at the Apollo 13 radio call, and 'reported' is not asking for a sound here

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reported' is the trap, because it almost always calls for a homophone. Here it belongs to the picture — the famous line sent up from a crippled spacecraft.
explanation.definitionFit: worry → PROBLEM: the thing on your mind that needs solving is your problem, the everyday sense in which a worry and a difficulty are one and the same.

clue.text: Is oiler able to go finally, with America picking quarrels?

definitions.note: The definition is a participle phrase where the answer is a plain adjective: a cantankerous person is one forever picking quarrels, so the phrase describes the answer rather than swapping straight in for it.

indicators.note: What comes finally is what stands at the very end, so only the last letter of the little word beside it is taken.

blocks.note: if you are able to do something you can do it
an oiler is a ship carrying oil, which is a tanker
the closing letter of that two-letter word
US is the country's initials standing in for the whole name

explanation.walkthrough: Read as English it is a question about a ship leaving port, and that is the whole of the misdirection: no piece moves anywhere, they simply follow one another as given.
explanation.definitionFit: picking quarrels → CANTANKEROUS: a cantankerous neighbour is bad-tempered and contrary, forever finding something to argue about.

clue.text: French bread you proved, one hears

definitions.note: The definition is a mass-noun idiom — bread for money is uncountable — while the answer is a plural, and the enumeration is what gives that away.

indicators.note: What is heard rather than read is a sound, so the two words before it are to be said aloud and written down some other way.

blocks.note: the pronoun is a single sound, and dough that has proved has risen — it rose

explanation.walkthrough: 'French bread' is money rather than a baguette: bread is old slang for cash. The bakery is there only to make 'proved' sound like something out of a recipe.
explanation.definitionFit: French bread → EUROS: bread is slang for money and the money in France is the euro, so the two words together name a currency, not a loaf.

clue.text: Giant gnome gardener keeps inside

indicators.note: What somebody keeps inside is not on show, so the letters are held whole within the words rather than spelled out by them.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.walkthrough: A garden gnome is exactly what the surface wants you to picture, and the definition is the one word in the clue with nothing to do with gardens.
explanation.definitionFit: Giant → MEGA: mega is the informal adjective for enormous, the unit prefix meaning a million doing service as slang.

clue.text: Last month city turned greener, to announce start of campaign

indicators.note: A word turned is facing the other way, so the piece beside it is read from its end back to its start.

blocks.note: December is the last of the twelve, and DEC is how a diary prints it
LA is Los Angeles in two letters, the way a ticket writes it
a greener hand is a rawer one, less experienced, and it arrives back to front

explanation.walkthrough: 'Greener' is a comparative about inexperience rather than about the environment, and the city is the same one 17 across comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: announce start of campaign → DECLARE WAR: declaring war is the formal announcement that a military campaign has begun, so the phrase reads almost literally.

clue.text: See 5
National emblem that's terrifying on lieutenant's face

indicators.note: In an across entry a piece sitting on another comes straight after it, so the cry follows the letter it lands on.
A word's face is the front it shows the world, which is the letter it begins with.

blocks.note: the front letter of the rank, which is also how the rank is abbreviated
the noise a frightened character makes in a comic strip

explanation.walkthrough: 'National emblem' could be almost anything, so this one is solved from the wordplay end: a rank's opening letter and the squeal of a startled cartoon.
explanation.definitionFit: National emblem → LEEK: the leek is the national emblem of Wales, worn on St David's Day alongside the daffodil.

clue.text: Old lady spat on Republican, giving tissue

indicators.note: In an across entry a thing landing on another sits directly after it, so the quarrel follows the party's letter.

blocks.note: MA is the affectionate short form for a mother
R is the letter printed after an American Republican's name
a spat is a short quarrel, and a row is the noisier word for one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spat' looks like a past tense with someone doing the spitting, and it is a noun; the American party is in the clue for its initial and nothing else.
explanation.definitionFit: tissue → MARROW: marrow is the soft tissue filling the middle of a bone, so the definition names the general class it belongs to.

clue.text: Yeti wanders around some blasted mountain wilderness

indicators.note: A creature that wanders around keeps to no fixed route, and neither do these letters once they have been picked up.
Something blasted has been blown apart, so the little word beside it is shattered into loose letters as well.

blocks.note: the beast's name is raw material, not a character in the story
the vague-looking word is fodder too, four more letters for the pile

explanation.walkthrough: Two indicators and two lots of fodder sit side by side, which is why it reads so smoothly as a sentence about a monster on a mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: mountain wilderness → YOSEMITE: the California national park of granite cliffs and high Sierra country, defined here by the kind of place it is.
